article_text:
Daniel Weiss had a part-time job as a stock clerk in the gift shop at the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C., while in school at George Washington University studying psychology and art history. When his boss was fired for substantial revenue losses, Weiss told the people in charge at the Kennedy Center: “I think I can fix this.” He was offered a six-month tryout the week he graduated in 1979, and over the next four years continued to run the retail business and supervise a staff of 175.

It wouldn’t be the last time he stepped in to fix things.

“Along the way, I realized I was interested in pursuing graduate training in art history, but I also had an interest in how organizations function,” Weiss said this summer at the Philadelphia Museum of Art , where he started as director and CEO last December, a month after the board of trustees fired his predecessor, Sasha Suda. While at the Kennedy Center and throughout “the rest of my career,” he explained, “it became clear to me that if one cares about culture and the arts and higher education, one has an obligation to care also about how these institutions are run.”

Weiss, now 69, is widely viewed as a smart and thoughtful straight shooter, skilled at solving organizational problems. With an MBA from Yale and a PhD in Western medieval and Byzantine art from Johns Hopkins, he had a long career in academia, working in tandem as president and professor at Lafayette and then Haverford colleges, before being hired as president and chief operating officer of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 2015. In his eight years at the Met, he helped steer the institution out of a $40 million financial deficit and through a change in directors and internal culture. Now at the PMA, which is also facing a major budget deficit after years of high staff turnover and low morale, Weiss is being looked to as a steady hand to right the ship.

“Dan brings a combination of qualities that’s uncommon,” said PMA board chair Ellen Caplan. “He obviously understands art and scholarship, but also how to lead large, complex organizations. He has a proven track record and a compelling vision for the role that museums play in society right now.”

When Weiss stepped down from the Met in 2023, his plan was to teach, write books, spend time on his boat, and, he said, “just live the life of somebody who wakes up not in charge of anything.” He took a faculty position at Johns Hopkins, where he had begun his teaching career in 1993, and was asked by several institutions, including the PMA—on Suda’s introduction—to advise on governance practices. “I’m something of a voice in that area,” said Weiss, who articulated his views on the importance of shared governance at mission-driven institutions in his 2022 book Why the Museum Matters .

Working with the PMA’s board on a governance review over the next two years, Weiss “got to watch, from a fairly close point of view, the dissolution of Sasha’s relationship with the institution and the board,” he said. After Suda’s termination in November 2025, according to the public record, she filed a lawsuit contending that she was fired “without a valid basis,” and pushed to have a jury trial; the board responded that “Suda misappropriated funds from the museum and lied to cover up her theft.” A court ruled early this year that the matter would be settled privately in arbitration, as per a clause in Suda’s contract.

The board’s decision to terminate Suda was made “completely independent of anyone that we were going to bring in to follow up,” Caplan said. “One had nothing to do with the other.”

Weiss said that at first, when the board approached him to step in, he was hesitant to take the helm. “My initial reaction was: ‘I’m not your guy,’” he recalled. “On the other hand, I thought, I know how to do this. I understand the issues. Maybe we can get this place back on track, where it’s doing what it should in the world.”

According to a veteran of the New York museum world, speaking on background, Weiss’s replacement of Suda could have at least the appearance of opportunism. “Dan, who is a consultant to the board, slip[ped] into that job really quickly. He has a way of being like a board whisperer,” said the person, adding, “I’m not saying that there weren’t reasons for both Dan to accept it and the board to do what they were doing. Things are never that black and white.”

Asked if the PMA board had considered conducting a search for a new director, vice chair Osagie Imasogie said the trustees had unanimously agreed to appoint Weiss to the position. “If you look at the market for top-notch leaders in museums of the caliber of the PMA, it’s just a handful of people who would fit that profile,” he said. “There was no point in going through a performative process when we already had the best person we could think about.”

If the board had brought Weiss in on only an interim basis, that would have diminished “the full authority to get on with the work that needs to be done,” Imasogie added. “It was also important that we ensure stability be brought back to the institution after the challenges we have had.”

In his work with the governance committee, Weiss had presented to the full board. “There was an immediate comfort level, both because we knew Dan,” said Jennifer Rice, chair of the governance committee at the time, and “he also came with such a stellar reputation for the work he did at the Met.”

DURING AN INTERVIEW OVER LUNCH in his office, Weiss came across as direct and efficient, at once businesslike, candid, and personable. Before addressing the first question he was posed, he paused to point out that, like his interviewer, he, too, wore a coin on a chain, pulling from underneath his shirt and tie a third-century Hellenistic coin with the image of Alexander the Great, given to him by his family. “I’ve worn it around my neck for 25 years,” he said. “It feels like a connection to the ancient world and the continuity of human existence.”

Born in Newark, New Jersey, and raised on New York’s Long Island, Weiss described himself as “a completely lackluster student” early on. Wandering into an art history survey class at GW, he fell under the spell of a charismatic young professor who was a medievalist. “He changed my life,” said Weiss, who is friends with him to this day. “That was where it began for me.” With his dual graduate training in art history and business, Weiss began teaching at Johns Hopkins as well as writing books; by the time he was tenured, he’d also become involved in administrative work. “I knew how to run a meeting and had experience in things that most faculty don’t,” he said. He rose to the position of dean in 2001, before moving in 2005 to lead Lafayette College for eight years, then Haverford College for two. He described being very surprised when the Met approached him.

“I’d never worked in a museum before, and they were asking me if I wanted to run it,” Weiss said. “They were looking for someone who could bring management and fiscal knowledge and experience into a role that was also completely sympathetic and sensitive to the mission. It opened up a world for me that I didn’t really plan on.”

In his first weeks on the job, he dug into the museum’s financial statements and discovered that what had been presented to him as a modest $4 million deficit on a budget of more than $300 million was, in fact, a $40 million deficit.

“The museum was drawing down reserves in ways that weren’t really kosher to meet operating deficits,” he said. “We had been overspending and, as it were, undermanaging the institution, and it had resulted in various patterns of accommodation to these problems that were not fully transparent to the board.”

Under Tom Campbell, a former tapestries curator promoted in 2009 to director and CEO after the retirement of Philippe de Montebello, who had led the Met for more than 30 years, the museum had been investing heavily in its digital operations as well as its modern and contemporary satellite, Met Breuer (which operated in the former Whitney building from 2016 to 2020).

“To Tom Campbell’s credit, I made him aware right away of a very substantial deficit, and he was perfectly willing … to do whatever it took to figure it out,” Weiss said.

Campbell would ultimately resign under pressure in 2017. The Met’s board voted unanimously that Weiss would assume the title of president and CEO, and that a new director would report to him. Max Hollein was appointed to that role in 2018, and by 2020, working together, the two leaders had balanced the budget. When Weiss stepped down in 2023, Hollein assumed the additional title of CEO.

“Dan is a leader who doesn’t shy away from complex issues,” said Candace Beinecke, cochair of the Met’s board. “His tenure at the Met was defined by his tremendous commitment to the museum’s mission. Working in partnership with the museum’s director, he steadily and effectively helped lead the Met through crucial moments. He brings deep analytical skills, expertise, and a strong sense of purpose to his work.”

Central to Weiss’s management at the Met was his reinforcement of the principles of shared governance. “It starts with the relationship between the CEO and the board,” he said, “but all the constituencies that have a vested interest in the well-being of the institution—the curators, the professional staff, the mayor’s office, the unions—also need to have a voice.”

Weiss enlisted the staff as partners in helping to fix the deficit, creating a task force of some 15 representatives to advise on budgetary decisions. They were part of tough conversations about how to cut the program, cut salaries, make layoffs. Weiss’s proposed changes to the museum’s longtime admissions policy of “pay what you wish”—after a decline of 67 percent in the average fee people paid during the previous decade—was controversial internally. The task force gave presentations to every department to involve the staff of 2,000 in the logic of Weiss’s proposition.

“We went through a long, difficult process to find the right approach based on principles, economic interest, and what’s best for the institution,” Weiss said. The new policy, instituted in 2018, maintained “pay what you wish” for New York State residents, who already support the Met through their taxes, but charged $25 (since raised to $30) for out-of-town adults. “In the end, it generated the revenue we needed, and it had no negative effect on visitation,” he said. “It was one step of 40 that we had to do to bring the budget into balance.”

A longtime Met employee, speaking on background, described Weiss as popular overall with the staff. “He was accessible, somebody you could talk to,” the employee said. “He’s a very rational, reasonable, and reasoned man.”

Weiss also instituted a review process at the Met, requiring the board to evaluate his own performance annually and perform a “360”—including feedback from employees—every other year. He later required the same for all department heads at the Met. “You must be accountable to the people you lead,” he said, noting that nobody would ever have given de Montebello a review. “I think it was a great disservice to Tom Campbell, who was a brand-new leader with no experience, not to have a performance evaluation of any kind.”

What Met trustee and former board chair Daniel Brodsky appreciated most in working with Weiss was “his willingness to listen,” he said. “He made time for staff at every level of the museum, and he genuinely cared about creating an environment where they could do their best work. During a period that included leadership transitions and the pandemic, that steady approach served the museum well.”

The PMA—RANKING IN THE TOP FIVE largest encyclopedic art museums in the US by both physical and collection size—now stands to gain from Weiss’s brand of leadership.

In late July, The Philadelphia Inquirer reported that the museum had a deficit of $10 million on an operating budget of $76.5 million and that its leadership expected the deficit could grow to as much as $15.9 million in the next year. Weiss said his goals for his first year are to fully assess the museum’s finances, rebuild the senior leadership team, and move forward on an action plan with open lines of communication across the board and staff.

In 2020, during the tenure of Timothy Rub, who led the PMA from 2009 to 2022, more than 400 staff members signed a petition calling for accountability changes in the wake of complaints about the behavior of former managers. Later that year, the staff voted to unionize. Museum workers went out on strike in 2022, on Suda’s first day on the job as new director (she chose to cross the picket line).

“Over the last several years, staff levels have decreased very dramatically,” Weiss said, from some 500 employees five years ago to about 385 now, through a combination of attrition, firings, and layoffs to reduce operating costs. “At the same time, the programmatic ambition during Sasha’s years here was very high, so there was more to do and fewer staff to do it. That led to a really strong sense of disappointment and frustration.”

Weiss has recently recruited Mitchell Wein, from the Brookings Institution, as executive vice president, chief financial officer, and chief operating officer; Lavita McMath Turner, from the Met, as chief people officer; and Neil Batiancila, from the Philadelphia Zoo, as chief advancement officer. He’s also promoted longtime curator Jennifer Thompson to deputy director of collections and exhibitions, to work alongside Jessica Smith, chief curator.

“I didn’t want a hiring freeze when I arrived, because the institution couldn’t survive that way—you have to have people in the right jobs,” Weiss said, acknowledging that he had added to the expense base. “We’ll balance the budget—it’s just a matter of exactly how. I know what the levers are.”

Caplan said that Weiss’s consistent internal communication on his action plan—addressing nine areas, including facilities, visitor experience, technology, and security—has already helped with morale. “He’s continuing to provide updates on progress being made or challenges he’s facing, and that transparency is appreciated by both the staff and the trustees,” she said.

Weiss appointed an internal task force to reevaluate a controversial rebranding campaign rolled out last fall under Suda, which included the institution’s name change to the Philadelphia Art Museum (mocked by critics as “the PhArt Museum”). A collaborative decision was made early this year to reinstate the original name but keep the new logo, featuring a griffin—a decorative architectural element repeated across the museum’s 1928 Beaux-Arts building.

The plan for a second phase of an ambitious expansion—originally approved by the board in 2004, during the tenure of Rub’s predecessor, Anne d’Harnoncourt, then designed by the late Frank Gehry—is now on hold. (The first phase of the plan was completed under Rub in 2021, for $233 million.) “We have a series of deferred building maintenance issues that have to be addressed before we return to the question of the Gehry project,” Weiss said.

He believes the museum’s current annual attendance of about 675,000 is “way too low,” he said, given the size and quality of the institution’s world-renowned collection of more than 240,000 objects and its stature in the city. But he has yet to set a specific target number for visitation, or dig into the question of admissions cost. “We feel very strongly that admissions pricing is a necessary evil, but whatever we do has to work for Philadelphia, so people come,” he said. The museum’s endowment—now almost $600 million—could always be better, Weiss said, but “it’s totally respectable.”

Weiss, who has committed to staying through 2028, told The Philadelphia Inquirer that he expects to have the budget balanced in three years. He and the board will then decide whether he will continue on for longer, he said, stating firmly, “I’m not going to stay 10 years.” He and his wife, a corporate healthcare lawyer whom he met at GW, live near the museum in a high-rise building. In Easton, Maryland, where he serves on the board of the Academy Art Museum, among several other institutions, they have a second home, with an extensive book collection that reflects Weiss’s diverse interests. His boat remains docked in the marina there.

While the skills of museum leadership may be transferable, Weiss recognizes that he is “not operating on the same patient,” he said. “The PMA is not the Met. They have different issues, different cultures, different communities. You need to listen very carefully and take what you know and apply it respectfully to this place in this ecosystem. I don’t have it all figured out.”

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://www.filmcritics.org.hk/sites/default/files/2026-11/Artboard%2030.png", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "香港電影評論學會"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "香港電影評論學會現誠徵節目及宣傳統籌一職（全職工作），招聘詳情如下。 職位名稱：節目及宣傳統籌 ( Programme & Promotion Coordinator) 行業類別：電影 / 藝術文化 / 活動策劃 工作類型：全職 (12 個月合約)  職位概述： 我們正在尋找一位對電影充滿熱誠、具備創意及注重細節的「節目及宣傳統籌」加入我們的團隊。你將在電影放映活動及文化項目的「行政統籌」與「創意宣傳」工作中扮演關鍵角色。如果你熱愛電影，同時擁有良好的行政與設計能力，歡迎加入學會。 工作內容： 節目及活動統籌 協助電影放映活動及文化項目的協調與行政工作，處理活動的籌備、安排及物流等； 與電影發行商聯絡及磋商，申請版權、片源及收集電影相關宣傳資料和電影資訊； 安排電影拷貝的運送事宜，包括電影發行商與本會及放映場館之間的檔案傳輸、實體拷貝運輸安排、清關、與貨運公司聯絡等，確保電影拷貝可準時抵達放映場地； 統籌電影字幕的事宜，包括安排和追蹤字幕翻譯的進度、協助編輯、校對和查核字幕、協助放映當日的字幕投放； 場地預訂及聯絡，準備電影排期、申請電檢及票務事宜； 統籌海報設計、節目手冊排版、印刷及分發； 統籌節目映後談和本會組織的其他活動； 如有需要，須於戶外及不定時工作 宣傳及社交媒體管理 策劃、編寫、設計宣傳物料及管理各大社交媒體平台（如 Instagram、Facebook、YouTube）的宣傳內容，協助推廣學會活動、出版、網店及網頁，提升觀眾互動率。 撰寫、編輯及校對具吸引力的市場營銷文案、新聞稿及節目簡介。 監察宣傳活動的效果，並協助收集觀眾反饋意見。 入職條件： 香港特別行政區永久性居民，並持有大學學位或同等之學歷；擁有1年或以上的電影節目相關經驗； 具翻譯或編輯經驗者將優先考慮； 須具備優良中、英文語言能力；能操流利廣東話； 能獨立工作、具責任心、組織及承受壓力，能靈活應變及處理電影節目、學會其他活動及宣傳工作； 對電影及文化事務有熱情及一定認識； 須熟悉電腦操作、文書處理。熟悉操作設計軟件（包括 Adobe Illustrator (AI)、Photoshop、等）者將獲優先考慮。 應徵方法： 有意者請將個人履歷、設計作品集（Portfolio）或文字範本、現時及期望薪酬，以及可到職日期，電郵至 [email protected] ，註明「應徵宣傳及節目統籌」。 截止日期：2026年11月30日 合適者將獲通知安排面試。（註：建議申請人儘快提交申請，申請人之篩選及面試將會即時展開，至有關職位空缺被填補即止。）若申請人於截止日期後8個星期內仍不獲通知面試，其申請將作落選論。  (申請人所提供的資料將予保密及祇作招聘有關職位用途。）", "links": [{"text": "[email protected]", "url": "https://www.filmcritics.org.hk/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection"}]}]

title_original: Behind the Scenes with the Architects of Aperture’s New Home
editorial_title_zh: 走进 Aperture 新址建筑师的幕后世界
editorial_excerpt_zh: 建筑事务所 LEVENBETTS 的斯特拉·贝茨（Stella Betts）与大卫·莱文（David Leven）分享了新空间的细节——从拥抱建筑历史到创造“Aperture 灰”。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "本周，Aperture 在纽约哥伦布大道 380 号迎来了新址的开幕。这家书店兼画廊坐落于上西区一栋历史建筑的前两层，是一个人们可以聚集、分享想法并接触摄影的场所，也将成为举办一系列充满活力的公共活动的平台。", "links": [{"text": "dynamic series of public programs", "url": "https://aperture.org/editorial/a-season-of-public-programs-at-apertures-new-home/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aperture 新址的设计由屡获殊荣的建筑事务所 LEVENBETTS 主导。在这里，斯特拉·贝茨与大卫·莱文深入探讨了关于我们新空间的 5 个鲜为人知的事实，从拥抱建筑历史到“Aperture 灰”这一绰号。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Aperture_091526_016-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Aperture_091526_025-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "建筑历史", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大卫·莱文：这座建筑是历史建筑；它大约在 1880 年代作为一栋名为 The Evelyn 的住宅楼建造。它由一位名叫埃米尔·格鲁韦（Emile Gruwe）的建筑师以某种文艺复兴复兴风格设计。在研究期间，我们发现 Aperture 空间的一部分最初是多个公寓的餐厅和厨房区域。这里曾是那些自己公寓里可能没有厨房的居民做饭和用餐的地方，旁边还有公共壁炉等等。这是一个社交空间。我们为 Aperture 创建的入口就位于这个区域。我们对这种社交性和社区感的理念很感兴趣，它现在从过去延续到了现在，但在建筑中以一种新的方式被重新诠释。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Aperture_091526_044-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Aperture_091526_027-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "书店与画廊", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "斯特拉·贝茨：书店空间真正的主旨是庆祝 Aperture 创作的书籍和杂志。它是面向公众的门面，至关重要的是，当你走在街上时能真正看到它，并且一从大厅进来就能具备可见性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "莱文：一进来，你就会看到书架和公共空间。这个空间将举行讲座和活动，届时我们可以搬入椅子并放下投影幕布。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "店内的货架线条非常纤细，以此作为对砖墙粗糙质感的某种并置。我们考虑了它们可以做到多细、多极简，同时还能承载将要放入这里的全部书籍的重量。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们还与 Aperture 馆长萨拉·迈斯特（Sarah Meister）进行了大量讨论，关于是将画廊和活动区域刷成白色，还是保留或移除多少内容，什么该清理或保留。最后，我们一致决定，我们真的很想保留原建筑的痕迹和个性。而且我认为这与这里将要展出的摄影作品仍然配合得很好，几乎与建筑本身形成了对话。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Aperture_091526_030-1-1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "强调现有材料", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贝茨：当我们最初为 Aperture 的未来新址寻找潜在空间时，我认为搬到上西区有点像是一次跨越。在过去二十年左右的时间里，Aperture 一直位于切尔西，甚至曾将目光投向苏荷区和其他街区。我们所有人对这个空间和位置爱不释手的原因在于它的个性和历史。我们希望继续捕捉市中心阁楼的感觉——大卫称之为“空间的粗粝感”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为了做到这一点，我们努力保留了某种建筑历史。就我们对摄影的热爱而言，这也是一个非常重要的方面，它关乎讲述故事。这个项目的重要之处在于讲述这座建筑的故事，而不是抹去这段历史。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "莱文：我们进行了许多精彩的对话，探讨到底保留多少、移除多少、清理什么、保护什么。这里有支撑着数千磅重量的钢铁过梁。到处都是原汁原味的拱门、痕迹和砖砌结构。这一切都归结为历史和故事的理念。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贝茨：设计过程的一个重要部分是对每一面墙进行编目。我们对每一面墙进行了照片记录，并就某些东西要清理到什么程度做出了决定。例如，许多墙壁保留了所谓的瑕疵，这些瑕疵在其他项目中会被移除。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Aperture_091526_053-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Aperture_091526_041-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aperture 灰", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贝茨：我们采用了我们称之为“植入（insertions）”的方法，即我们在空间中进行增补，使其区别于现有空间。这些植入部分采用了一种我们亲切地命名为“Aperture 灰”的色调，它部分基于摄影的区域曝光法（Zone System）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "莱文：这也是为了不在色调和所见的物品中添加太多其他元素。浅浅的 Aperture 灰颜色隐入空间之中，但它也无处不在：门框都是同一个颜色的。书架都是同一个颜色的。桌子也采用了这种颜色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贝茨：书籍本身将使空间充满活力，画廊里也会有摄影作品。因此，对我们来说，我们的想法是让建筑与摄影和书籍共存，而我们所做的增补则采用这种中性的 Aperture 灰。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Aperture_091526_017-1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "所有图片均来自 Aperture 书店与画廊，2026 年。克里斯·格雷夫斯（Kris Graves）摄影", "credit": "Aperture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "光的平等", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贝茨：Aperture 的新址分为上下两层，因此你需要为下层和上层都提供光线，我们非常希望所有区域都能获得某种程度的共享光线或直接光线——即光的平等。透明度的理念也非常重要。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "楼下有一些非常厚重、质感极美的石质地基墙。虽然有窗户，但地下一层无法像楼上那样获得充足的光线。为了让光线产生漫反射，我们决定将整个楼下刷成白色——同时保留那种原始的质感。我们在设计过程中的对话，非常像是去寻找一种罗伯特·雷曼（Robert Ryman）式的白底白画，你只得到单一的调色板色彩，但却能欣赏到墙壁本身的质感。这一切都回归到了建筑的性格上。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "This week, Aperture opens the doors of its new home at 380 Columbus Avenue in New York City. Situated on the first two floors of a historic building on the Upper West Side, the bookstore and gallery is a place to gather, share ideas, and engage with photography, and will be a platform for a dynamic series of public programs .", "links": [{"text": "dynamic series of public programs", "url": "https://aperture.org/editorial/a-season-of-public-programs-at-apertures-new-home/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Design for Aperture’s new home has been led by the award-winning architecture practice LEVENBETTS. Here, Stella Betts and David Leven dive into five lesser-known facts about our new space, from embracing the building’s history to the nickname “Aperture Gray.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Aperture_091526_016-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Aperture_091526_025-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "History of the Building"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "David Leven: The building is historical; it was built in the 1880s or so as a residential building called The Evelyn. It was designed by an architect named Emile Gruwe in a kind of Renaissance Revival fashion. During our research, we discovered that part of Aperture’s space was originally dining and kitchen areas for multiple apartments. It would have been a place for cooking and dining for residents who may not have had kitchens in their own apartments, alongside communal fireplaces and so on. It was a social space. The entry we have created for Aperture is located in this area. We were interested in this idea of socialness and community, which has now been carried from the past to the present, but reinterpreted in a new way within the architecture."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Aperture_091526_044-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Aperture_091526_027-scaled.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Bookstore & Gallery"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Stella Betts: The bookstore space is really about celebrating the books and the magazine that Aperture does. It’s the public face, and it was vital that you really see it when you’re on the street, and that there’s a visibility as soon as you enter from the lobby."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Leven: As soon as you come in, you’re seeing bookshelves and the public space. There will be talks and events that happen in this space, where we’re able to bring in chairs and a projector screen that comes down."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The shelving in the store has very thin lines, as a kind of juxtaposition to the roughness of the brick walls. We took into consideration how thin and minimal they could be and still carry the weight of all the books that are going to go in here."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There was also a lot of discussion with Sarah Meister, Aperture’s director, about whether to paint the gallery and programs area white, or how much do we leave or take away, what gets cleaned or left. In the end, we all decided that we really wanted to keep the markings and the character of the original building. And I think that that still works well with the photography that will be shown here, almost becoming in dialogue with the building itself."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://aperture.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Aperture_091526_030-1-1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Aperture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Emphasizing the Existing Materials"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Betts: When we were initially looking at potential spaces for Aperture’s future home, I think the idea of moving to the Upper West Side was a little bit of a leap. For the past twenty years or so Aperture had been located in Chelsea and had even set its sights on SoHo and other neighborhoods. What we all fell in love with about this space and location is the character, the history. And we wanted to continue to capture a downtown loft feeling—what David calls “the rawness of the space.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "To do this, we made an effort to leave a sort of history of the building. That’s also a really important thing for us in terms of what we love about photography, it’s about telling stories. What was significant with this project was to tell the story of the building and to not remove that history."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Leven: We’ve had so many great conversations about how much do we leave, how much do we take away, what gets cleaned, what gets preserved. article_text:
This week, Aperture opens the doors of its new home at 380 Columbus Avenue in New York City. Situated on the first two floors of a historic building on the Upper West Side, the bookstore and gallery is a place to gather, share ideas, and engage with photography, and will be a platform for a dynamic series of public programs .

Design for Aperture’s new home has been led by the award-winning architecture practice LEVENBETTS. Here, Stella Betts and David Leven dive into five lesser-known facts about our new space, from embracing the building’s history to the nickname “Aperture Gray.”

History of the Building

David Leven: The building is historical; it was built in the 1880s or so as a residential building called The Evelyn. It was designed by an architect named Emile Gruwe in a kind of Renaissance Revival fashion. During our research, we discovered that part of Aperture’s space was originally dining and kitchen areas for multiple apartments. It would have been a place for cooking and dining for residents who may not have had kitchens in their own apartments, alongside communal fireplaces and so on. It was a social space. The entry we have created for Aperture is located in this area. We were interested in this idea of socialness and community, which has now been carried from the past to the present, but reinterpreted in a new way within the architecture.

Bookstore & Gallery

Stella Betts: The bookstore space is really about celebrating the books and the magazine that Aperture does. It’s the public face, and it was vital that you really see it when you’re on the street, and that there’s a visibility as soon as you enter from the lobby.

Leven: As soon as you come in, you’re seeing bookshelves and the public space. There will be talks and events that happen in this space, where we’re able to bring in chairs and a projector screen that comes down.

The shelving in the store has very thin lines, as a kind of juxtaposition to the roughness of the brick walls. We took into consideration how thin and minimal they could be and still carry the weight of all the books that are going to go in here.

There was also a lot of discussion with Sarah Meister, Aperture’s director, about whether to paint the gallery and programs area white, or how much do we leave or take away, what gets cleaned or left. In the end, we all decided that we really wanted to keep the markings and the character of the original building. And I think that that still works well with the photography that will be shown here, almost becoming in dialogue with the building itself.

Emphasizing the Existing Materials

Betts: When we were initially looking at potential spaces for Aperture’s future home, I think the idea of moving to the Upper West Side was a little bit of a leap. For the past twenty years or so Aperture had been located in Chelsea and had even set its sights on SoHo and other neighborhoods. What we all fell in love with about this space and location is the character, the history. And we wanted to continue to capture a downtown loft feeling—what David calls “the rawness of the space.”

To do this, we made an effort to leave a sort of history of the building. That’s also a really important thing for us in terms of what we love about photography, it’s about telling stories. What was significant with this project was to tell the story of the building and to not remove that history.

Leven: We’ve had so many great conversations about how much do we leave, how much do we take away, what gets cleaned, what gets preserved. There are steel lintels holding up thousands of pounds. There are original archways and markings and brickwork throughout. It all goes back to this idea of the history and story.

Betts: A big part of the design process was cataloging every single wall. We photo-documented each wall and made decisions in terms of to what degree certain things were going to be cleaned. For example, many of the walls retain so-called imperfections that in other projects would be removed.

Aperture Gray

Betts: We took this approach of what we are calling “insertions,” where we’re adding to the space and making it distinct from the existing space. These insertions were created in a palette that we affectionately named “Aperture Gray,” which was partially based on the photography Zone System.

Leven: This was also in order to not add too many other elements within the palettes and things you see. The light Aperture Gray color recedes into the space, but it’s also omnipresent throughout: the doorframes are all the same color. The bookshelves are all the same color. The desks pick up that color.

Betts: The books themselves will animate the space, and there’ll be photography in the gallery as well. So, the idea for us was to let the building be present with the photography and books, and the additions that we’ve made are in this neutral Aperture Gray.

Equity of Light

Betts: Aperture’s home has a split between two floors, so you need light for both the lower level and the upper level, and we really wanted to have all areas have some degree of shared light or direct light—an equity of light. The idea of transparency also was really important.

Downstairs there are some very thick, heavy stone foundation walls that have beautiful texture. Although there are windows, the lower level doesn’t get the same amount of light as the upper floor. In order for the light to bounce, we decided to paint the entire downstairs white—while keeping that original texture. When we had conversations during the design process it was very much like seeking a kind of Robert Ryman white-on-white painting where you get just a single palette color, but you get to enjoy the texture of the wall itself. It all goes back to the character of the building.
